title: How B-2 Pilots Eat, Sleep & Go to the Bathroom on a 44-Hour Mission
asof: Figures from the 2001 and 2025 missions · sources in description

shots.s: Two pilots. One seat each.
And no one to take over for forty-four hours.
The cabin is about the size of a closet.
There's a tiny toilet in the back.
A cot on the floor.
And you're flying halfway around the world, and back.
So how do you eat,
sleep,
and go to the bathroom,
inside a B-2 bomber?
This is the B-2 Spirit.
It's a flying wing, about fifty-two meters across.
It was built to slip past radar.
Only twenty-one were ever built.
They all fly from one base, Whiteman, in Missouri.
The jet was designed for a crew of up to three.
It flies with two pilots.
One of them is also the mission commander.
With air refueling, the jet can keep going.
The limit isn't fuel.
The limit is the two people inside.
October 2001.
Two pilots, Mel Deaile and Brian Neal, take off from Missouri.
Their target is in Afghanistan.
They fly west, across the Pacific.
Their mission lasts forty-four point three hours.
One of them later said:
there is no preparation, no simulator, for a forty-four-hour mission.
The only bed is behind the seats.
On that 2001 flight, it was a modified Army cot.
And a sleeping bag.
Today, the Air Force says, pilots can nap on a metal surface back there.
And it isn't comfortable.
One pilot sleeps while the other flies.
But both must be in their seats for the hard parts.
Deaile said it wasn't high-quality sleep.
But at that point, any sleep is good sleep.
Before a mission, pilots work with an aerospace physiologist.
For days, they shift their sleep to match the flight.
On earlier missions, pilots also took go pills, to stay awake.
Deaile said they speed up your heart.
It is not a fun feeling.
The B-2 can't land to refuel.
So it meets tankers in the air.
A boom reaches down from the tanker,
and plugs into the top of the jet.
Each connection takes about thirty minutes of total focus.
Pilots describe finishing drenched in sweat.
In the dark, in clouds or turbulence, it's even harder.
Deaile said the mission wasn't about Afghanistan.
It was about reaching the next tanker on time.
Miss one, and the mission is over.

card: THE GAS STATION IN THE SKY

shots.s: There's no galley.
There is a microwave.
Pilots bring whatever food they want.
On the 2001 flight: coffee,
sandwiches,
pretzels,
and pre-packed meals made for eating in flight.
But sitting for that long, nobody gets very hungry.
The air up there is extremely dry.
The jet makes its own oxygen from outside air.
That leaves almost no moisture in the cabin.
So pilots drink, and drink.
The Air Force says even so, skin dries out and cracks.
And all that water has to go somewhere.
The B-2 has one small chemical toilet.
It couldn't hold forty-four hours' worth.
So the crew used piddle packs.
Plastic bags with a powder that turns urine into gel.
Deaile said they filled about two an hour.
Then they did the math.
How many pounds of gel would they have to unload?
There's no shower.
No change of clothes, either.
Over the flight suit go a harness, a life vest and a survival vest.
Changing would take too long.
The 2001 mission ran long.
Controllers asked them to go back over Afghanistan.
Then a plane ahead had an emergency, so they circled.
Finally, they land on Diego Garcia, an island in the Indian Ocean.
Deaile said they were just glad to be back on solid ground.
In June 2025, seven B-2s flew about thirty-seven hours to strike Iran.
The second-longest B-2 mission ever.
Same two seats. Same tiny toilet.
Could you stay awake for forty-four hours in a closet?
